newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks may celebrate election only briefly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks may celebrate election only briefly.

text.p: The 1996 U.S. federal election, which again matches a Democratic President with a Republican Congress, is likely to be greeted with a brief victory party on Wall Street followed by profit-taking.
"The problem is that it's been fully discounted by the market," said Hugh Johnson, strategist at First Albany Co.
"You could get a light applause tomorrow morning, but then I wouldn't be surprised to see the adage 'buy on the rumor, sell on the news' take hold."

"I think there will be a 'sigh of relief,' really, that lasts maybe half an hour," said Michael Metz, market analyst at Oppenheimer & Co. He said the election outcome, continuing the status-quo of Democrat Bill Clinton in the White House with Republicans controlling the Senate and House of Representaives, was "what a lot of investors were waiting for and hoping for."

The Republican challenger, Bob Dole, conceded defeat just before 1130 EST Tuesday and predicted the Republicans would retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Final tallies confirming that the Republicans would hang on to majorities in both houses were not expected for several hours.

"The market has had two strong days," said Robert Stovall of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers. He noted the Dow industrials rose 20 points Monday and another 40 points the following day to finish Tuesday at 6081. The Dow was close to its all-time closing high of 6094 reached on October 18.
Analysts said Tuesday's gain was clearly tied to anticipation of the election results.
The view on Wall Street is that divided government keeps a brake on spending and thus has contributed to the U.S. budget deficit getting smaller over recent years.

Chuck Spence, a vice president for treasury sales at Standard Chartered Bank in New York, said the election result would go over well with foreign investors, who pay close attention to progress or lack of progress in controlling the deficit.
He said the dollar would probably trade higher against the yen and European currencies, and any pullback in stocks would be seen by foreigners as a buying opportunity.
Spence said foreigners have become "quite comfortable" with Clinton's move toward the political center after Republicans won control of the House and Senate two years ago.
After the dust from the election settles, investors may be looking at economic trends and corporate prospects which make the outlook for the intermediate term cloudy, analysts said.
Johnson said the long expansionary phase in the U.S. economy may finally peter out in 1998 and investors could be taking notice of that in mid-1997.

Metz said a huge expansion in profit margins for U.S. corporations appears to have run its course. He also noted that the dollar has been in an upward trend, and this could be a problem for U.S. manufacturers as their goods become more expensive overseas.

Stovall said that records going back to 1832 show than when a U.S. president is re-elected, the stock market does not do well the following year. One excepton was the re-election of Ronald Reagan in 1984 which was followed by a bouyant market.

Stovall noted that "exit polls" of voters on U.S. television showed many are aware of and troubled by accusations about President Clinton's ethics. The continuation of investigations could even weigh on the market in the future, he said.

Separately, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce issued a statement welcoming the projected Republican retention of both houses of Congress, saying it would provide a pro-business counter-balance to the Clinton Administration.
